The morning light spills softly across the quiet kitchen table.
Steam rises from a chipped blue cup of jasmine tea.
Outside, sparrows argue over crumbs near the rusty garden gate.
I watch their tiny shadows flicker against the weathered wall.
Memory arrives uninvited, wearing the face of an old friend.
We once walked barefoot through wet streets laughing at thunder.
That laughter still lives beneath my ribs, warm and sudden.
Books pile on chairs like tiny continents awaiting quiet exploration.
A pencil snaps beside a notebook filled with unfinished plans.
Some dreams are seeds; others are only beautiful, patient dust.
The clock above the doorway ticks as if counting mercy.
I forgive the yesterday that frightened me with its silence.
Tomorrow can keep its questions folded inside little paper cranes.
For now, the tea cools, and the world asks nothing.
Sunlight climbs the shelf, touches a photograph, then slips away.
In the picture, we are young and squinting at summer.
We did not know how quickly joy would become nostalgia.
Yet grief is not the price of loving ordinary days.
It is simply the shadow cast by attention and time.
I choose to notice the bread, the bird, the breath.
Small things gather like stars into a constellation I hold.
The gate creaks open; a neighbor waves from the street.
I wave back, feeling strangely grateful for this unremarkable morning.
Perhaps peace is not a destination but a daily returning.
So I sit and let light finish what it began.
